newsitem.title: USA: Close U.S.-Japan ties vital to stability - Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Close U.S.-Japan ties vital to stability - Rubin.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Monday that good relations with Japan remained a cornerstone of U.S. economic and political strategy in the Pacific.

"With our countries being the two largest economies in the world and together representing one-third of world GDP, an effective working relationship ... (is) key to the stability and prosperity of not only Japan and the United States but the entire region and the global economy," Rubin said in a speech prepared for delivery to the Japan Society in New York.
A text was issued in advance in Washington.
Rubin said he was "deeply troubled" by an apparent retreat from support at home for policies that promote U.S. international engagement.

"I believe that it is absolutely vital to our national interest to reverse that retreat," he said. Rubin said representatives from other industrial nations regularly express their concern to him about the U.S. direction as evidenced by arrears to the United Nations and the World Bank.
Global integration was a fact of life, Rubin said, and U.S. economic success depended upon joining the regional alliances and sectoral agreements that characterize the world economy.
Rubin noted that Japan has suffered through five years of weak economic performance, in contrast to U.S. strength during the same period, and suggested some remedies for Japan.
"Excessive government regulation, restrictive informal business practices, and markets that are relatively closed to foreign competition reduce competitiveness, investment and growth," he noted.

He urged Japan to pursue policies to boost domestic demand and avoid piling up big trade surpluses. Rubin warned that if Japan let its current account surplus mount to levels that harm global growth it would fuel trade frictions and protectionism in other countries.
